nodes.title: Physical Layer Function
nodes.description: The physical layer is the first and lowest layer of the OSI model and is responsible for carrying bits across a physical transmission medium.

nodes.title: Analog and Digital Signals
nodes.description: An analog signal varies continuously and smoothly over time, whereas a digital signal uses discrete values, commonly represented as LOW and HIGH or 0 and 1.

nodes.title: Bit Rate and Bit Length
nodes.description: Bit rate is the number of bits transmitted per second, while bit length is the physical distance occupied by one bit in a medium. Higher bit rates pack more bits into a given transmission distance.

nodes.title: Physical Layer and Signal Fundamentals
nodes.description: Explains the physical layer's role in carrying bits and introduces the basic forms and measurements of transmitted signals.

nodes.title: Digital Modulation and Encoding Assumptions
nodes.description: Digital modulation converts bits into signals and received signals back into bits. The introductory model assumes discrete high and low signals for encoding binary 1 and 0.

nodes.title: Non-Return to Zero and Desynchronization
nodes.description: Non-Return to Zero represents 1 with a high signal and 0 with a low signal. Long sequences without transitions make receiver clock recovery difficult and can cause desynchronization.

nodes.title: Non-Return to Zero Inverted
nodes.description: NRZI represents a binary 1 by making a signal transition and a binary 0 by leaving the signal unchanged.

nodes.title: Manchester Encoding
nodes.description: Manchester encoding uses a high-to-low transition for 1 and a low-to-high transition for 0, providing regular transitions that support clock synchronization.

nodes.title: 4-bit/5-bit Encoding
nodes.description: The 4-bit/5-bit technique maps four-bit data groups into five-bit codes to prevent problematic sequences of zeros when used with NRZI, including in 100 Mbps Ethernet.

nodes.title: Differential Encoding Strategies
nodes.description: Differential encoding represents data through changes in signal state rather than relying only on absolute voltage levels.

nodes.title: Digital Data Encoding Techniques
nodes.description: Examines how binary data is converted into physical signals and the synchronization properties of major line-encoding methods.

nodes.title: Synchronous Transmission

nodes.title: Transmission Impairment Overview
nodes.description: Transmission impairments are effects that degrade signals as they pass through a medium, principally attenuation, distortion, and noise.

nodes.title: Attenuation
nodes.description: Attenuation is the loss of signal energy as a signal travels through a transmission medium, resulting in a weaker received signal.

nodes.title: Distortion
nodes.description: Distortion occurs when a signal changes its form or shape, particularly when components of a composite signal propagate differently.

nodes.title: Noise
nodes.description: Noise is unwanted energy that interferes with a signal during transmission. The material introduces multiple noise types, including thermal noise caused by random electron motion.

nodes.title: Transmission Impairments

nodes.title: Nyquist Formula
nodes.description: The Nyquist formula determines the maximum bit rate of a noiseless channel from its bandwidth and number of discrete signal levels: Maximum Bit Rate = 2B log2 L.

nodes.title: Shannon Formula
nodes.description: The Shannon formula determines channel capacity in the presence of noise using bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio: Channel Capacity = B log2(1 + SNR).

nodes.title: Guided and Unguided Transmission Media
nodes.description: Transmission media provide the path over which signals travel and are classified into guided media, which constrain signals to a physical path, and unguided media, which transmit through free space.

nodes.title: Twisted Pair Cable
nodes.description: Twisted-pair cable contains two individually insulated conductors, usually copper. Its applications include telephone lines and low-cost LANs, and its forms include Unshielded Twisted Pair and shielded variants.

nodes.title: Coaxial Cable
nodes.description: Coaxial cable uses concentric conductors and carries higher-frequency signals than twisted pair. It provides higher bandwidth and strong noise immunity for communication applications.

nodes.title: Fibre Optic Cable and Propagation Modes
nodes.description: Fibre-optic cable uses a glass or plastic core and transmits information as light. Its propagation modes depend on the core and lower-density cladding, and the medium offers high bandwidth and low attenuation alongside stated disadvantages and applications.

nodes.title: Wireless Propagation Methods
nodes.description: Unguided transmission uses electromagnetic waves traveling through free space. Propagation methods include ground propagation, in which lower-frequency radio waves follow the curvature of the Earth.

nodes.title: Radio Waves
nodes.description: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves in the approximate frequency range of 3 kHz to 1 GHz and are used for wireless communication.

nodes.title: Microwaves
nodes.description: Microwaves occupy the approximate frequency range from 1 GHz to 300 GHz and are used as an unguided communication medium.

nodes.title: Infrared
nodes.description: Infrared communication uses frequencies of approximately 300 GHz to 400 THz and is suited to short-range communication.

nodes.title: Switching Networks and Switching Methods
nodes.description: A switching network is a collection of interconnected nodes and connections used for communication. Data can be switched using circuit switching or packet switching, with packet switching divided into datagram and virtual-circuit approaches.

nodes.title: Switching Network Foundations
nodes.description: Defines a switching network and identifies the principal methods used to move data through interconnected nodes.

children.title: Switching Networks and Switching Methods
children.description: A switching network is a collection of interconnected nodes and connections used for communication. Data can be switched using circuit switching or packet switching, with packet switching divided into datagram and virtual-circuit approaches.

nodes.title: Circuit Switching
nodes.description: Circuit switching establishes a dedicated communication path through circuit establishment, data transfer, and circuit disconnection phases. It can be inefficient because channel capacity remains dedicated for the connection's duration.

nodes.title: Packet Switching
nodes.description: Packet switching divides a long message into packets and sends the packets through the network individually, allowing network resources to be shared.

nodes.title: Datagram Packet Switching
nodes.description: Datagram switching is connectionless: no route is established before transmission, and individual packets may be handled independently.

nodes.title: Virtual Circuit Packet Switching
nodes.description: Virtual-circuit switching establishes a planned route before packets are sent, providing a connection-oriented path for the packet sequence.

nodes.title: Applied Comparison of Switching Methods
nodes.description: Review questions evaluate virtual-circuit behavior, the inefficiency of idle dedicated circuits, and the greater resource efficiency generally provided by packet switching.
